title: Low credibility URL sharing on Twitter during reporting linking rare blood clots with the Oxford/AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine
screen_reason: Reports four verbatim shares of tweets/shared links that referenced low-credibility domains, each with an explicit denominator (0.28% and 1.9% for the COVID corpus; 0.72% and 2.9% for the AstraZeneca corpus). The study's own framing is 'low credibility URL sharing', so these are SHARING content-share estimates.

estimates.country: Not reported (multilingual global Twitter stream; keyword list covers seven languages; authors state 'this research did not look at where the Twitter users were based')
estimates.measure_type: % of all COVID-19-related tweets that referenced a low-credibility domain
estimates.denominator: 36.5 million COVID-19-related tweets and retweets collected 4-25 March 2021 from a continuous 1% keyword-filtered sample of the Twitter API (keywords in seven languages)
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if it contained a URL whose domain appears on the March 2021 Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo list of domains that regularly publish misinformation or disinformation.
estimates.misinfo_def: "The Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo dataset (the Iffy+ List) is a list of domains that regularly publish misinformation or disinformation collated using lists of low-credibility sources from independent fact-checking organisations Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC), FactCheck.org, and PolitiFact; digital media organisation BuzzFeed; and online encyclopaedia Wikipedia"
estimates.source_quote: We identified 100,708 COVID-19-related tweets which referenced low-credibility domains (0.28% of all COVID- 19-related tweets, and 1.9% of those containing URLs)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo list, March 2021 version, 812 domains; compiled from Media Bias/Fact Check, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, BuzzFeed and Wikipedia; verifies sources in 19 languages including the seven in the study's keyword list. No per-item human coding; authors note the approach 'almost certainly underestimates the scale of misinformation by omitting false or misleading information spread through the body of tweets or comments, or references to low-credibility sources which were not included on the Iffy+ List'.
estimates.moderator_quote: To identify low-credibility information propagating on Twitter, this research focuses on the sharing of URL domains which have been identified as routinely publishing low-credibility information. This methodology has been widely adopted across the literature.
estimates.notes: The widest denominator the paper reports: all COVID-19-keyword tweets, whether or not they contain a URL. Because only URL-bearing tweets can possibly be classified low-credibility, this figure mechanically depends on the 14.5% URL rate; the companion row restricted to URL-containing tweets (1.9%) is the like-for-like 'share of shared links' figure. Corpus is a 1% API sample, so counts are a sample, not a census. QUOTE NOTE: the source_quote reproduces the text file exactly, including the PDF line-break hyphenation artefacts ('COVID- 19-related', 'ref- erenced'); in the article these read 'COVID-19-related' and 'referenced'.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted as a CONCENTRATION row (fails R1): 'RT.com is a dominant source of low-credibility content, constituting nearly 20% of all low-credibility COVID-19-related URLs, and over 40% of all low-credibility AZ-related URLs shared in the study period.' This is a single top source with a stated share of sharing (conc_unit=source, conc_dimension=sharing), but the paper never reports how many distinct low-credibility domains appeared in the data, so conc_group_pct cannot be filled, and both values are approximations ('nearly 20%', 'over 40%') rather than exact points. Flagging for the adjudicator: if a source-level conc_group_pct can be assigned (e.g. 1 of the 812 domains on the Iffy+ list = 0.12%, which I judge to be the wrong denominator), two CONCENTRATION rows could be added. Also relevant: RT.com was referenced 647 times in the Peak period vs 178 and 238 Pre- and Post-Peak in the AZ corpus, and childrenshealthdefence.org 12 times Pre-Peak vs 238 in the Peak period - bare counts, unusable. 2) NOT extracted: 14.5% of COVID tweets and 24.9% of AZ tweets contained URLs, and AZ tweets were 0.9% of COVID tweets - denominators/structure of the corpus, not misinformation shares. 3) NOT extracted: Table 3 retweet rates (e.g. Low-Credibility AZ 8.05% / 17.4% / 11.0% across Pre-Peak / Peak / Post-Peak) - the share of tweets that were retweeted, i.e. engagement, not the share of content that is misinformation. 4) NOT extracted: Table 4 network composition (e.g. Low-Credibility COVID 7.8% Authors / 80.9% Sharers Pre-Peak) - account role composition. 5) NOT extracted: Table 8 verified-account proportions (Userbase 1.5% vs Top 100 influential low-credibility Authors 39%) and account-creation shares (25% of the Userbase, 18% of Influential Low-Credibility Authors, 11% of Influential Residual Authors created since 11 March 2020) - account attributes, not misinformation prevalence, though the verified/follower contrasts are relevant background for who spreads it. 6) NOT extracted: 'potential exposure' means (Table 2: COVID low-credibility 17,000 users/tweet vs 24,000 for residual; AZ 15,000 vs 40,000). These are mean potential audience per TWEET (sum of author follower counts), not exposure per person, so they are not a per-capita intensity of exposure to misinformation and have no interpretable denominator of people; the authors themselves say it 'is neither an upper nor lower bound of the actual exposure'. 7) Time-period breakdowns: the paper gives Pre-Peak / Peak / Post-Peak splits only in figures for the low-credibility shares, so the three-week totals are the only extractable point estimates (consistent with the instruction to collapse a time series to one representative point). 8) Country is genuinely unknown: the authors explicitly did not geolocate users, and note the AZ vaccine was not used globally.

rob.design: Non-probability platform corpus, source-level classification. Frame: continuous automated retrieval of a 1% sample of tweets containing COVID-19 keywords (keyword list in seven languages, S1 Table) via the Twitter API; tweets containing URLs posted 4-25 March 2021 were selected, spanning the week before, of, and after the UK peak of media coverage linking AZ to blood clots (11-17 March 2021). 36.5M COVID-19-related tweets, of which 5.3M contained URLs; an AZ keyword filter produced 336,483 AZ tweets (83,646 with URLs). Classification: no human coding - a tweet is 'low-credibility' if its URL domain is on the March 2021 Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo list (812 domains, assembled from MBFC, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, BuzzFeed and Wikipedia); no inter-rater reliability applicable. Network analysis with NetworkX/Gephi; in-degree, out-degree and eigenvector centrality; significance by Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis. Author-declared limitations: Twitter users are not representative (younger, more male); broad keywords admit off-topic tweets (a visible contamination from an unrelated Nigerian trending topic via the keyword 'ICU'); the domain-list method 'almost certainly underestimates' misinformation because it cannot see false claims in tweet text; retweet chains are not preserved; exposure is only 'potential'; only seven languages; no geolocation.
rob.item6_quote: The Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo dataset (the Iffy+ List) is a list of domains that regularly publish misinformation or disinformation collated using lists of low-credibility sources from independent fact-checking organisations Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC), FactCheck.org, and PolitiFact; digital media organisation BuzzFeed; and online encyclopaedia Wikipedia [18].
rob.item10_quote: We identified 100,708 COVID-19-related tweets which referenced low-credibility domains (0.28% of all COVID-19-related tweets, and 1.9% of those containing URLs); and 2,419 AZ-related tweets which referenced low-credibility domains (0.72% of all AZ-related tweets, and 2.9% of those containing URLs).
